title: The family it started
lede: Steak and Ale’s competitors were, to an unusual degree, its own descendants: a sibling created inside the same company, a founder’s second act, and chains started by former employees.

blocks.title: Who won, who died
blocks.subtitle: Steak and Ale and the chains closest to it.

items.name: Steak and Ale
items.text: Closed in the 2008 Chapter 7. One restaurant has operated under new owners since 2024.[^1][^8][^37]

items.name: Bennigan’s
items.text: Created by Brinker in 1976 and sold with Steak and Ale in 1989. Lost its company restaurants in 2008; franchisees kept the name alive.[^4][^5][^32]

items.name: Chili’s (Brinker International)
items.text: Brinker left Pillsbury in 1983 for a small hamburger chain and built it into one of the largest restaurant companies in the world.[^2][^6]

items.name: Outback Steakhouse
items.text: Its co-founders Tim Gannon and Chris Sullivan worked at a Steak and Ale in Maryland in 1973.[^25]

items.name: Ponderosa and Bonanza
items.text: Metromedia’s budget steakhouses, paired with Steak and Ale in the abandoned 2003 sale. Their company filed for Chapter 11 three months after S&A.[^13][^23]

blocks.source: Counts from The New York Times[^1][^2], Nation’s Restaurant News[^4][^6], Restaurant Business[^32], The Dallas Morning News[^8][^25] and company releases.[^23] They are for different years and are not a like-for-like comparison. We have no sourced count for Outback and give none.

blocks.title: Who invented casual dining
blocks.body: A 2018 Bennigan’s menu said Steak and Ale “created casual dining,” and the owners say it introduced the salad bar to casual dining.[^31][^37] Nation’s Restaurant News replied that the first claim “is open to debate”: the first T.G.I. Friday’s opened in New York in 1965, a year earlier, though it was then more a bar than a restaurant.[^31] The New York Times credited Brinker more cautiously with having “helped put casual dining and salad bars on the American menu.”[^2]

blocks.text: All these bar and grill concepts are very, very similar. They have the same kind of menu, décor, appeal.
blocks.who: Bob Goldin, executive vice president of Technomic, The New York Times, Jul 30, 2008[^3]
